questions.question: Which 1798 joint volume by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge is treated as the opening manifesto of English Romanticism?
questions.explanation: Wordsworth and Coleridge co-published 'Lyrical Ballads' anonymously in 1798, launching the English Romantic movement.

questions.question: The conventional closing year of the Romantic Period in 1832 is marked by the death of Sir Walter Scott and the passage of:
questions.explanation: The year 1832 marks the end of the Romantic era with Sir Walter Scott's death and the First Reform Act under Earl Grey.

questions.question: Which 1785 blank-verse poem by William Cowper contains the famous line 'God made the country, and man made the town'?
questions.explanation: William Cowper published 'The Task' in 1785, contrasting rural virtue with urban corruption.

questions.question: Which Scottish poet, known as 'The Ploughman Poet', published 'Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect' at Kilmarnock in 1786?
questions.explanation: Robert Burns published his landmark Kilmarnock Edition, 'Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect', in 1786.

questions.question: In which 1785 Scots lyric did Robert Burns write 'The best-laid schemes o' mice an' men / Gang aft agley'?
questions.explanation: Robert Burns composed 'To a Mouse' in 1785 after turning up a mouse's nest with his plough.

questions.question: Which Romantic poet and engraver invented 'Illuminated Printing' to etch text and illustrations together on copper plates?
questions.explanation: William Blake invented Illuminated Printing, hand-etching and hand-colouring his poems and visionary designs on copper plates.

questions.question: William Blake published 'Songs of Innocence' in 1789 and combined it in 1794 with which companion collection?
questions.explanation: Blake published 'Songs of Innocence' in 1789 and added 'Songs of Experience' in 1794 to show the two contrary states of the soul.

questions.question: In William Blake's 'Songs of Innocence and of Experience', which pair of companion poems contrasts gentle and terrifying creation?
questions.explanation: Blake paired 'The Lamb' from Innocence with 'The Tyger' from Experience as contrary visions of creation.

questions.question: In which 1794 poem from 'Songs of Experience' does William Blake condemn 'charter'd' streets and 'mind-forg'd manacles'?
questions.explanation: Blake's 'London' in 'Songs of Experience' protests urban misery, institutional oppression, and mind-forged manacles.

questions.question: The French Revolution began in July 1789 with the storming of which medieval fortress-prison in Paris?
questions.explanation: Parisian citizens stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789, an event initially celebrated by British Romantic writers.

questions.question: Who authored 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' (1790), launching the conservative attack on the French Revolution?
questions.explanation: Edmund Burke published 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' in November 1790, defending inherited tradition and monarchy.

questions.question: Which radical writer defended the French Revolution against Edmund Burke in 'Rights of Man' (1791–1792)?
questions.explanation: Thomas Paine answered Burke's 'Reflections' with Part I and Part II of 'Rights of Man' in 1791 and 1792.

questions.question: Who wrote the foundational feminist treatise 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' in 1792?
questions.explanation: Mary Wollstonecraft published 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' in 1792, arguing for women's rational education.

questions.question: Which philosopher published 'An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice' in 1793, advocating philosophical anarchism?
questions.explanation: William Godwin published 'An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice' in 1793, influencing Wordsworth, Coleridge, and Shelley.

questions.question: What name did Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Robert Southey give to the egalitarian community they planned in the 1790s?
questions.explanation: In the 1790s Coleridge and Southey planned Pantisocracy, an equal communal society to be established in America.

questions.question: In the 1800 Preface to 'Lyrical Ballads', how did William Wordsworth famously define all good poetry?
options: 'A speaking picture with the end to teach and delight'
'The best words in the best philosophical order'
'An imitation of nature in rhymed heroic couplets'
questions.explanation: Wordsworth's 1800 Preface defines poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings from emotion recollected in tranquility.

questions.question: In the Preface to 'Lyrical Ballads', William Wordsworth rejected artificial poetic diction and defined the poet as:
questions.explanation: Wordsworth described the poet in his Preface as a man speaking to men in a selection of language really used by men.

questions.question: Which reflective blank-verse poem by William Wordsworth concluded the first edition of 'Lyrical Ballads' in 1798?
options: 'Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey'
questions.explanation: Wordsworth's meditative poem 'Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey' closed the 1798 edition of 'Lyrical Ballads'.

questions.question: Which blank-verse autobiographical epic by William Wordsworth was completed in 1805 but published posthumously in 1850?
questions.explanation: Wordsworth's autobiographical poem 'The Prelude' was published after his death in 1850 by his widow Mary.

questions.question: William Wordsworth's 'Ode: Intimations of Immortality' (1802–1804) mourns the fading of the visionary splendour of:
questions.explanation: Wordsworth's Immortality Ode laments the passing of childhood's celestial light while finding philosophical consolation in nature.

questions.question: Which sonnet by William Wordsworth begins 'The world is too much with us; late and soon, / Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers'?
options: 'The World Is Too Much with Us'
questions.explanation: Wordsworth's sonnet 'The World Is Too Much with Us' criticizes commercial materialism for alienating humanity from nature.

questions.question: By what collective name were William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and Robert Southey known due to their residence in northwest England?
questions.explanation: Wordsworth, Coleridge, and Southey lived in the Lake District and were grouped together as the Lake Poets.

questions.question: In Samuel Taylor Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798), what bird does the Mariner shoot, bringing a curse upon his ship?
questions.explanation: The Ancient Mariner shoots an auspicious albatross, giving English the idiom an albatross around one's neck.

questions.question: Which visionary fragment by Samuel Taylor Coleridge (published 1816) was reportedly interrupted by 'a person on business from Porlock'?
questions.explanation: Coleridge stated that 'Kubla Khan', composed in an opium dream around 1797, was interrupted by a visitor from Porlock.

questions.question: Which unfinished medieval supernatural poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge was published alongside 'Kubla Khan' in 1816?
questions.explanation: Coleridge's unfinished gothic ballad 'Christabel' was published in his 1816 volume with 'Kubla Khan'.

questions.question: In which 1817 critical work did Samuel Taylor Coleridge distinguish 'Fancy' from 'Imagination' and coin 'willing suspension of disbelief'?
questions.explanation: Coleridge published 'Biographia Literaria' in 1817, introducing willing suspension of disbelief and his theory of Imagination.

questions.question: Coleridge's 'This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison' and 'Frost at Midnight' are prominent examples of which poetic group?
questions.explanation: Coleridge's quiet, meditative blank-verse poems addressed to friends or family are called his conversation poems.

questions.question: With which 1809 verse satire did Lord Byron retaliate against the harsh review of his first volume, 'Hours of Idleness' (1807)?
questions.explanation: Lord Byron published 'English Bards and Scotch Reviewers' in 1809 to counter Edinburgh critics of 'Hours of Idleness'.

questions.question: Which long narrative poem (1812–1818) made Lord Byron famous overnight and established the archetype of the 'Byronic hero'?
questions.explanation: Byron's 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage' made him famous in 1812 and defined the brooding, alienated Byronic hero.

questions.question: What is the title of Lord Byron's unfinished satirical epic in ottava rima (1819–1824), regarded as his comic masterpiece?
questions.explanation: Byron's 'Don Juan', composed in ottava rima between 1819 and 1824, is his greatest satirical epic.

questions.question: Lord Byron died of fever at Missolonghi on 19 April 1824 while actively supporting the War of Independence in:
questions.explanation: Byron sailed to Greece in 1823 to aid the Greek War of Independence against Ottoman rule and died at Missolonghi in 1824.

questions.question: Why was Percy Bysshe Shelley expelled from Oxford University in 1811 along with his friend Thomas Jefferson Hogg?
options: For co-authoring the pamphlet 'The Necessity of Atheism'
For organizing the Luddite machine-breaking uprising
For publishing a seditious libel against the Prince Regent
For fighting a pistol duel against an Edinburgh reviewer
questions.explanation: Shelley was expelled from University College, Oxford, in 1811 for refusing to disavow 'The Necessity of Atheism'.

questions.question: Which 1818 sonnet by Percy Bysshe Shelley describes a ruined desert monument bearing the words 'Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!'?
questions.explanation: Shelley's 1818 sonnet 'Ozymandias' uses a shattered statue in the desert to expose the transience of tyrannical power.

questions.question: Which 1819 ode by Percy Bysshe Shelley concludes with the famous line 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?'?
questions.explanation: Shelley's 'Ode to the West Wind' of 1819 invokes the autumn wind as both destroyer and preserver, ending with the prophecy of Spring.

questions.question: Who authored the four-act lyrical drama 'Prometheus Unbound' (1820) and the five-act verse tragedy 'The Cenci' (1819)?
questions.explanation: Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote the tragedy 'The Cenci' in 1819 and the mythological lyrical drama 'Prometheus Unbound' in 1820.

questions.question: What is the title of Percy Bysshe Shelley's 1821 pastoral elegy written to mourn the death of John Keats?
questions.explanation: Shelley composed 'Adonais' in 1821 as a pastoral elegy mourning John Keats's death in Rome.

questions.question: Which August 1819 massacre of peaceful parliamentary reform protesters at St. Peter's Field, Manchester, inspired Shelley's 'The Masque of Anarchy'?
questions.explanation: On 16 August 1819 cavalry charged peaceful protesters at St. Peter's Field in the Peterloo Massacre, prompting Shelley's poem.

questions.question: Which 1818 four-book poetic romance by John Keats opens with the famous line 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever'?
questions.explanation: Keats's 1818 poem 'Endymion: A Poetic Romance' begins with the celebrated declaration that a thing of beauty is a joy for ever.

questions.question: Which year is celebrated as John Keats's 'Great Year', when he wrote 'To Autumn', 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', and 'Ode to a Nightingale'?
questions.explanation: In a few months of 1819, his Great Year, Keats composed his major odes, 'The Eve of St. Agnes', and 'Hyperion'.

questions.question: Which critical phrase did John Keats coin in an 1817 letter for the capacity to remain in 'uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts'?
questions.explanation: Keats coined negative capability in a December 1817 letter to his brothers, praising Shakespeare for possessing this quality.

questions.question: John Keats died of tuberculosis in Rome in February 1821 at age 25 and asked that his tombstone bear which epitaph?
options: 'Nothing of him that doth fade, but doth suffer a sea-change'
'Here lies one whose name was writ in water'
'A poet of beauty resting in eternal sleep'
'Awake, forever awake, beneath the Roman sky'
questions.explanation: Keats died in Rome on 23 February 1821 and chose the epitaph Here lies one whose name was writ in water.

questions.question: Jane Austen's novel 'Pride and Prejudice' (1813), portraying Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy, was originally drafted under what title?
questions.explanation: Jane Austen drafted 'Pride and Prejudice' in the late 1790s under the working title 'First Impressions'.

questions.question: Which 1815 novel by Jane Austen centres on the well-meaning but misguided matchmaking schemes of its wealthy heroine?
questions.explanation: Jane Austen's 1815 novel 'Emma' follows the comic matchmaking blunders of its heroine, Emma Woodhouse.

questions.question: Which two novels by Jane Austen were published posthumously together in 1817, the year of her death?
questions.explanation: 'Persuasion' and 'Northanger Abbey' were issued together posthumously at the end of 1817.

questions.question: Which 1814 novel by Sir Walter Scott, set during the 1745 Jacobite Rising, is regarded as the first true historical novel?
questions.explanation: Sir Walter Scott published 'Waverley' anonymously in 1814, pioneering the modern historical novel.

questions.question: Which popular 1819 historical novel by Sir Walter Scott shifted his subject from Scottish history to 12th-century medieval England?
questions.explanation: Scott's 'Ivanhoe' of 1819 is set in 12th-century England during the reign of Richard the Lionheart.

questions.question: Who authored the 1818 Gothic-scientific novel 'Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus', conceived at Villa Diodati in 1816?
questions.explanation: Mary Shelley, daughter of William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft, published 'Frankenstein' anonymously in 1818.

questions.question: Under which pen name did Charles Lamb contribute his personal essays to 'The London Magazine' between 1820 and 1825?
questions.explanation: Charles Lamb used the pseudonym Elia, borrowed from an Italian clerk at the South Sea House, for his 'Essays of Elia'.

questions.question: Who wrote the autobiographical work 'Confessions of an English Opium-Eater', serialized in 'The London Magazine' in 1821?
questions.explanation: Thomas De Quincey published 'Confessions of an English Opium-Eater' in 1821, pioneering modern addiction literature.

questions.question: Which Romantic critic and essayist, friend of Lamb and Hunt, wrote sharp political and literary essays such as 'Table-Talk'?
questions.explanation: William Hazlitt was a leading Romantic essayist and critic closely connected to Lamb, Hunt, and Coleridge.
